title: Capacity in the Water Tray
strapline: Full, empty, half, overflowing — measuring the world by pouring it.
intent: Children explore capacity and volume through pouring, filling and emptying — maths you can feel in your hands.
Children build the language of quantity: full, empty, half full, nearly, too much, not enough, holds more.
Children compare containers and discover that tall and thin can hold the same as short and fat.
Children estimate and then test: how many cups fill the jug, will this bottle overflow that bowl?
Children strengthen the hand and wrist control that pouring, scooping and aiming demand.
implementation: Stock the water tray with a range of containers — jugs, bottles, cups, funnels, ladles — in clearly different sizes.
Model and feed in capacity words as you play: 'you filled it right to the top — it's full!', 'now it's empty'.
Pose pouring problems: 'how many little cups do you think will fill the big jug?' then count as they pour.
Set up a surprise: two very different-shaped containers that actually hold the same, and wonder which holds more.
Add coloured water or bubbles some days so the level is easy to see and talk about.
Extend to dry pouring too — rice, lentils, sand — so children compare how different materials behave.
Take it outside with buckets, guttering and a water butt for big-scale filling and emptying.
key_questions: Is it full or empty now?
How many cups do you think will fill the jug — shall we count and see?
Which container holds more — how could we find out?
What happens if you keep pouring?
Can you fill it exactly to halfway?

impact.text: Children use capacity language — full, empty, half, more, less.
Children compare containers to find which holds more or less.
Children estimate and then count how many cups fill a container.
Children pour, scoop and aim with growing hand control.
Children test an idea about capacity and talk about what they found.
Children stay absorbed, repeating and refining the pouring.

enhancements: Funnels, tubing, sieves and a water wheel to explore flow.
A dry version — lentils or rice — to compare with water.
Measuring jugs with clear markings for children ready to read a level.
Outdoor guttering and buckets for large-scale filling and emptying.
A pipette and small-bottle station for fine, careful pouring.
A 'potion lab' prompt — half a cup of this, fill to the top with that.

playing_exploring: Children pour and fill endlessly, absorbed in cause and effect.
They test their own questions about which holds more.
active_learning: Children repeat the filling to get the level just right.
They stay with the water tray for long, deeply involved stretches.
creating_thinking: Children predict how many cups it will take, then check.
They notice that shape and capacity aren't the same, and puzzle over it.
